adds.title: Playing dress-up: Four cross-dressers jailed in Oman — Roya News
adds.summary: Roya News (19 Sep 2018), on the Public Prosecution's announcement: a Salalah preliminary court sentenced two men to four years in jail and fined them OMR 3,000 each for cross-dressing and sharing photos of themselves in women's clothes on social media, and two further men to three years with the same fine for featuring in the video; the sentences fall under the July 2018 Omani Penal Code provision (Article 22), under which 'any male that appears in female clothing or demeanor' may be fined up to OMR 3,000 and jailed up to one year, with additional 'publishing immoral acts on social media' charges. The article notes these follow January 2018 arrests by the Royal Oman Police of a group of men for dressing as women after social-media photos circulated. It documents court-ordered imprisonment of gender-nonconforming people in Oman, but contains no information on where inside the prison system those convicted were housed.

records.note: No data was found on placement practice within Omani prisons: no gender-identity-based placement rule, no trans-specific custody unit, and no documented housing/segregation case for trans prisoners were located in two search rounds. The only documented imprisonment route for gender-nonconforming people is the 2018 Penal Code 'imitating the opposite sex' offence — Salalah court sentences of 4 and 3 years (Sep 2018) and the January 2018 Royal Oman Police arrests — and the reporting describes convictions, not in-prison housing conditions, so no placement finding can be stated.

adds.title: Uruguay to build prison for transgender inmates — MercoPress
adds.summary: MercoPress (29 Jul 2023), citing Uruguayan authorities and officials: as part of a new prison planned for Montevideo there will be a specific sector for the trans population, which Parliamentary Commissioner for the prison system Juan Miguel Petit called 'good news for a very vulnerable population' and estimated would be ready in less than two years. National Rehabilitation Institute (INR) Director Luis Mendoza told a parliamentary hearing that 'if the trans person enters the system they have the right to decide if they want to go to a men's or women's prison,' and that while trans women are currently placed in female prisons, cohabitation entails 'a whole process' of adaptation; he also noted the new women's prison at Punta de Rieles would for the first time account for the trans population, adding 'the laws are very advanced in Uruguay, but the mentality and infrastructure are not in line.' The article cites official figures of 14,965 people deprived of liberty, including 28 trans women and nine trans men (Office of the Parliamentary Commissioner for the Prison System).

records.note: Uruguay's documented placement practice is prisoner-choice-based: trans entrants may decide between men's and women's prisons, with trans women currently placed in female prisons (INR director, parliamentary hearing, Jul 2023), and a dedicated sector for the trans population was announced for a new Montevideo prison in Jul 2023 (status since then not documented in the sources found). Official counts: 28 trans women and nine trans men among ~14,965 prisoners. No court ruling on trans prison placement was located.

adds.title: Social News 16/1 — Separate jails proposed for transgender, gay prisoners
adds.summary: VietnamNet (16 Jan 2015) reports a proposal by the Social, Economic and Environmental Institute to Vietnam's Ministry of Public Security to house homosexual and transgender prisoners in jails separate from the general prison population, to protect them from sexual harassment; the institute cited US California statistics that 67% of homosexual and transgender prisoners had suffered sexual harassment and a 2014 survey finding that most transgender prisoners wanted separate jails. Critically for the placement lane, the institute stated that under Vietnam's then-current prison infrastructure transgender prisoners could only be held in solitary confinement or mixed with the general population — i.e. no housing wing matched to the prisoner's gender identity existed — and asked that prisoners be allowed to determine their own gender identity. No enacted outcome or newer documented placement practice was found in the two search rounds conducted.

records.note: No statutory placement-by-gender rule or gender-identity-based housing policy for transgender prisoners was found for Vietnam. The only documented placement-practice evidence located is the 2015 separate-jails proposal (VietnamNet, 16 Jan 2015): at that time transgender prisoners in Vietnamese prisons could only be placed in solitary confinement or mixed with the general population, a reform proposal was submitted to the Ministry of Public Security, and no enacted outcome is documented since. No trans-specific custody unit, court ruling on housing, or documented placement case (e.g., the 2019 Da Nang conviction coverage) was found that is verified as genuinely about this jurisdiction.
